The U.S. must respect India's right to defend itself and should maintain a zero-tolerance policy towards terrorism, former U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken said on Saturday (November 14, 2026), while describing Washington’s ties with New Delhi and Islamabad as “fundamentally different".
“India is a global force,” Mr. Blinken said, adding that the relationship and shared interests between Washington and New Delhi were “really global in nature”.
In contrast, the U.S. relationship with Pakistan is “regional," he said during a conversation with Jawed Ashraf, chairman of the India Trade Promotion Organisation, at a summit in New Delhi.
“ The relations with Pakistan are regional, and there are still going to be important areas where we need to do things with them, particularly, for example, when it comes to counter-terrorism, but these are fundamentally different relationships,” he said.
“We have to have a zero-tolerance policy for terrorism. Period. And that means that we have to have respect for India's right to defend itself,” he added.
Mr. Blinken said the U.S. approach must include support for India’s efforts to respond to attacks as well as diplomatic efforts to prevent an escalation between New Delhi and Islamabad, the two nuclear-armed neighbours.
He added that efforts to prevent escalation were important given the destructive potential of the weapons both countries possess.
Reflecting on Washington's past engagement with Islamabad, Mr. Blinken said U.S. strategic interests during the Cold War and the war in Afghanistan may have led successive administrations to be less critical of Pakistan's civil-military establishment.
“And there's certainly an opportunity for the United States to do more,” he added.
On India-U.S. relations, Mr. Blinken described the transformation in ties over the past few decades as a shift from estrangement to a strategic partnership, underpinned by shared interests and people-to-people connections.
“We moved from estrangement to a genuine and, in some ways, unique partnership, built on a convergence of strategic interests. Of course, it is also underpinned by the profound people-to-people connections between our societies,” he said.
He identified cooperation in emerging technologies as an important area for the two countries, pointing to collaboration in space, quantum technology and artificial intelligence.
“The next step is tech cooperation, our ability to work in space, tech, quantum, and artificial intelligence,” he said.
On India’s relations with Russia, Mr. Blinken acknowledged the partnership's historical depth and said Washington did not expect New Delhi to sever those ties.
“There will be places where we don't have the same perspectives. For Russia, we understand there is deep history between India and Russia. So, we don't want them to end it,” he said.
Mr. Blinken, who served as the 71st Secretary of State from 2021 to 2025 under then-President Joe Biden, said the world was at a profound inflection point, citing rapid technological change, inequality and shifting power.
“The speed and profundity of change is beyond anything we've seen, certainly in my lifetime,” he said, noting that ChatGPT, an Artificial Intelligence (AI) chatbot, took one month to reach 50 million users, compared with 75 years for the telephone.
He said the private sector increasingly drove technological change, while governments struggled to keep pace. Growing inequalities had fuelled a sense among younger people that they were being “left out, left behind", he said.
Mr. Blinken warned that the U.S. risked weakening its strength by damaging cooperation between the government, universities and research institutions, and by becoming less welcoming to skilled people from abroad.
“The biggest danger I think we face is a huge self-inflicted wound,” he said.
On U.S. domestic politics, Mr. Blinken said the recent midterm results went beyond the usual setback for the party of a sitting President. He attributed the outcome partly to frustration over the cost of living and concerns about corruption.
In the November 3 midterm elections, the Democratic Party won majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, shifting control of the US Congress away from Republicans.
Mr. Blinken described the U.S.-Israeli military campaign against Iran, launched in February by President Donald Trump, as “a war of choice" and said the first Trump administration’s withdrawal from the 2015 nuclear agreement with Tehran had contributed to the crisis.
He said the agreement, signed in 2015 and formally known as the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), required Iran to ship out 97% of its enriched uranium and placed limits on its centrifuges, while allowing extensive inspections.
After the U.S. withdrawal from JCPOA in 2018, Iran accelerated its nuclear programme, Blinken added, saying the ongoing military action would not resolve the issue.
“It is very hard to try to force this Iranian regime to capitulate; it is possible to get it to negotiate. And these are very different things,” he said.
He called for an “off-ramp” to the conflict, warning that escalation could involve attacks on regional infrastructure, US bases and partner countries.
The Strait of Hormuz, he said, had become a major challenge for global energy supplies after not being a problem before the war. Since February, Iran has repeatedly restricted access to the narrow chokepoint, one of the world's busiest oil shipping channels.
On the wider West Asia conflict, Mr. Blinken said a lasting settlement required resolving the Palestinian question and establishing a sovereign Palestinian state alongside a secure Israel.
“There are seven million Jews in Israel. There are seven million Arabs and Palestinians between Israel proper, the West Bank and Gaza. No one is going anywhere despite what extremists on both sides would like to see happen," he said.
"The solution remains, I fully believe, even though this is not a popular view, a secure Israel and a sovereign state of Palestine," he added.
